title: Does Telling an LLM to Be Concise Save Money?
hook: Two ways to spend fewer tokens: shorten what you send, or shorten what you ask for back. Measured across nine models, only one of them actually saves you money.
key_points: The study compares two levers on the same questions: compressing the input prompt versus instructing shorter output.
Both were tested at five reduction levels, scored on cost, accuracy, and fidelity to the unconstrained answer.
Result: compressing the output saves money while holding accuracy; compressing the input prompt does not save money.
Nine models were evaluated, including GPT-4o, GPT-5.4, and Claude Haiku 4.5.
Fidelity matters as much as accuracy — a shorter answer that no longer matches what the model would have said is a silent change, not a saving.
Practical read: output-length control (like a concise output style) is the lever with evidence behind it.
content_html: With a black-box model, the only two dials you really control are what goes in and how you ask for the answer back. This post reports a study that turns both dials on the same set of questions — shortening the input prompt versus instructing the model to answer more briefly — at five reduction levels each, scoring cost, accuracy, and whether the shortened text still matched what the model would have produced unconstrained.
extra_html:
The finding

The two channels are not symmetric. Compressing the output saves money and holds accuracy; compressing the input prompt does not deliver the savings. The evaluation spans nine models, including GPT-4o, GPT-5.4, and Claude Haiku 4.5. The authors frame it as timely because concise output styles are now shipping as product features — Claude Code added one — which makes it worth knowing which lever the evidence supports.

Reading it carefully

The fidelity check is the part worth internalizing. Accuracy can stay flat while the content of an answer shifts, so "shorter and still scores the same" and "shorter and still says the same thing" are different claims. See the linked post for the full methodology and the paper.

related.title: Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute
related.hook: A new scaling axis: instead of a bigger model, let a model think longer at inference — often a better use of compute, and the principle behind o1 and R1.

related.title: Learning When to Think: Adaptive Test-Time Compute
related.hook: Let the model pick its own thinking budget with its very first token. On MATH500 that cut response length 41% while accuracy barely moved.

related.title: Referential Dangling: How Prompt Compression Quietly Breaks Multi-Hop Answers
related.hook: Compressors score chunks independently, so they can keep the sentence holding the answer and delete the one defining who it's about — leaving text that reads fine and answers wrong.

flashcards.prompt: Which compression channel actually reduced cost in this study?
flashcards.explanation_html: Output compression saved money while keeping accuracy; compressing the input prompt did not produce savings.

flashcards.prompt: Besides cost and accuracy, what third thing did the authors score?
flashcards.back_html: Whether the shortened text still matched what the model would have said unconstrained — a shorter answer that quietly diverges isn't the same answer.

flashcards.prompt: Why is 'accuracy held steady' not enough to call a compression safe?
flashcards.back_html: Accuracy is a coarse aggregate. Content can shift while the score stays flat, which is why fidelity to the unconstrained response was measured separately.
